slides.title: What ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini actually are
slides.text: When you type into Google, Google goes to an index of pages that exist and gives you back links to those pages. When you type into ChatGPT, nothing like that happens. The model reads all the text in the conversation. Then it calculates what tiny piece of text is most likely to come next, and writes it. Then it rereads everything, including that piece it just wrote, and calculates the next one. Piece by piece, until…
items: Ask ChatGPT for the phone number of a famous restaurant with web search turned off. It'll give you a nine-digit number, perfect format, confident tone. It might be the real one or it might not exist at all: the model hasn't dialed that…

slides.title: Practice: Open all three and see the screen is the same
slides.text: Go to chatgpt.com, claude.ai, and gemini.google.com. On all three you can sign up free with your Google account by clicking "Continue with Google." Don't enter any card today: don't click "Upgrade plan," "Upgrade," or "Try Pro." With all three tabs open, notice all three screens look the same. A text box in the center and a list of past conversations on the left.
items: In your browser, three tabs
Three tabs, each with an empty chat and the cursor blinking in the text box. Zero charges to your card.

slides.title: Why it makes things up, and how to catch it in time
slides.text: Lying means knowing the truth and saying something else. That requires knowing it first. And inside there's no drawer full of facts, no little light that turns on when one is missing. There's a single operation repeating itself: given the text above, calculate what text fits below. When you ask it something that appeared a thousand times in what it read, what fits below is the correct answer, and it gets it right.…
items: Ask it for the customer service phone number of a small accounting firm in a random small town. It's never seen it in its life. It'll give you something like a real-looking phone number: correct area code, right number of digits, flawless…

slides.title: Practice: Trigger a fabrication with a blank question
slides.text: Open a new conversation with the "New chat" button (top left, pencil or square icon). It's important that it's new and empty. You're going to ask it about something that doesn't exist because you just made it up. Don't warn it about anything, don't tell it it's a test. Copy the message below exactly and paste it in the text box.

A summary with a plot, named characters, a page count, a publisher, and an award. All made up and all written without a hint of doubt. Pay close attention to the tone: it's identical to what it uses when telling you something true. That's…

slides.title: Why it forgets what you told it a while ago
slides.text: Every time you hit Enter, you're not talking to the same one that was there a while ago. The app takes the whole conversation from the first message, packs it into an envelope, and sends it back from scratch. It reads it in one pass, writes its answer, and everything gets erased. That stack of pages it rereads every turn is the context window (the chunk of text it can have in front of it at once), and it has a fixed…
items: In Marta's message 141, the AI reread all 140 previous ones in full before writing a single word. That's why it took 40 seconds to start when on day one it took 4.

slides.title: Practice: Measure how much room a text of yours actually takes up
slides.text: Open that address. You'll see a big empty text box. Take something real of yours — a long email you sent this week, a page of your notes, your idea's description — and paste it in. Right below the box, two numbers appear: "Tokens" and "Characters." The first is what it takes up on the AI's table. Now do the math: divide the tokens by your text's word count and you'll get something between 1.2 and 1.4. That's the…
items: In your browser, at platform.openai.com/tokenizer

Two numbers below the box. For an English text of about 500 words you should see between 600 and 700 tokens. Paste 10,000 words and you'll see about 13,000 tokens: that's about 6-7% of a 200,000 window, just from one document.

slides.title: Which AI to use for each thing
slides.text: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Copilot share 80% of whatever you're going to think of asking them. Drafting an awkward email. Explaining what a database is. Writing the code for a page with a contact form. All four do those things, and do them well. If you test a simple task on all four, the answers will look so similar you'll think it doesn't matter which one you use. The difference lives in the remaining 20%. That…
items: Same assignment to all three: write the homepage copy for a coffee shop. All three came back with something publishable in under twenty seconds and it was hard to pick. Second assignment: read these 180 customer emails and pull out the ten…

slides.title: Practice: Open the three free accounts in one sitting
slides.text: Go to chatgpt.com, claude.ai, and gemini.google.com. On all three, click the button top right. Depending on the page it says Sign up or Log in. Sign in with your Google account: it's the fastest and saves you inventing another password. None of them will ask for a card for the free plan. If a screen asking for a card number shows up, you clicked the upgrade plan button. Go back with the browser arrow. Leave all…
items: In your browser, three tabs
Three tabs with an empty text box waiting for you to type, and your name or initial top right on all three.

slides.title: How much this costs and how not to get a nasty surprise
slides.text: There are two ways to pay for AI, and confusing them is exactly what causes the scares. The first is subscription: you pay a fixed amount a month and use the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini app. When you hit the message limit, the app tells you to wait a while. It doesn't charge you a single extra cent. The second is pay-per-use, and it goes through the API. The API is the side door through which a program talks to the…
items: Marta didn't need the API to summarize her emails in the morning. She could paste them into Claude and read the summary, within her $25 subscription. She'd only need it if she wanted the summary to appear on its own at 8:00, with nobody at…

slides.title: Practice: Write down what you're already paying for AI
slides.text: Log into each with your account. Find your initial or your photo at bottom left or top right, click it, and go to "Settings." Inside, look for the section that says "Subscription," "Plan," or "Billing." Write down three things per service, on paper or in a note: which plan you have, how much you pay a month, and what day it renews. If it says "Free," write that too: it's just as valid information.
items: In your browser, on the site of each AI you use: chatgpt.com, claude.ai, gemini.google.com
A list of three or four lines like: "Claude — Pro — $20/mo — renews on the 14th." With that you now know your fixed AI spend, a number most people can't state off the top of their head.
